options: The built-in Windows console for reading the event logs Windows keeps automatically
A third-party tool that must be purchased separately to see any logs
A PowerShell module with no graphical interface
A log format used only by Linux systems
questions.explain: Event Viewer ships with every version of Windows and reads logs the OS is already writing whether anyone looks at them or not.

questions.q: Which Run-dialog command opens Event Viewer directly?
options: services.msc
gpedit.msc
secpol.msc
eventvwr.msc
questions.explain: eventvwr.msc opens Event Viewer from any Run dialog, remote session, or script — the fastest path once you know where you're going.

questions.q: Which three logs under Windows Logs carry most of the day-to-day weight?
options: System, Hardware Events, and Internet Explorer
Application, Security, and System
Security only — the other logs are rarely used
Setup, Forwarded Events, and Application only
questions.explain: Application logs app/service events, Security logs audit events, and System logs events from Windows itself and its core components.

questions.q: Why does reading the Security log require administrator rights, unlike Application or System?
options: Microsoft restricts it for licensing reasons unrelated to security
It only contains error messages from third-party applications
It records who logged on, who was created, and who was added to which group — sensitive account and privilege activity
It's actually not restricted at all — any user can read it freely
questions.explain: A non-admin who could freely read the Security log could map out account activity and privilege assignments on the machine, so it's locked to admins.

questions.q: In a logged event's General tab, what does the Event ID field tell you?
options: The exact time zone the server is configured for
The name of the administrator who configured the audit policy
A numeric code identifying exactly what kind of event was logged
The total number of events logged that day
questions.explain: Event ID is a numeric code identifying exactly what happened — filtering by it is the most common move when triaging a noisy log, and it's the focus of Lesson 10.
